name: Philoxenus of Mabbug
knownFor: Syriac bishop of Mabbug, also called Hierapolis, who fought the teaching of two natures in Christ and the Council of Chalcedon, pressed Flavian II of Antioch until Flavian was put out of his see in 512, by Budge's date, and wrote thirteen Discourses on the Christian life. He died in exile at Gangra.
dates: Born in the third quarter of the fifth century, in E. A. Wallis Budge's estimate. Made bishop of Mabbug in 485, by Budge's date. Driven from Mabbug in the second year of the emperor Justin, the year 830 of the Greeks, which Budge reads as 518 to 519. Died at Gangra. No early source used here gives the year of his birth or death; François Nau gives 523 as the end of his time as bishop
place: Tahal in Beth Garmai, his birthplace in Budge's account, a village a letter of Simeon of Beth Arsham names with him; Edessa, where Budge says he studied; Mabbug as bishop; Philippopolis in Thrace and Gangra in exile
role: Bishop of Mabbug; theologian and Syriac writer

keyWorks.title: Discourses, thirteen in number
keyWorks.about: on faith, simplicity, the fear of God, poverty, the lust of the belly, abstinence and fornication; Budge thinks they were written some years after 485 and before 500, since all their quotations come from the Peshitta

keyWorks.title: The version of the Bible made at Mabbug
keyWorks.about: Budge says a new Syriac translation of the four Gospels appeared at Mabbug in 508, and lists a version of the Old and New Testaments completed about then with the help of the chorepiscopus Polycarp, whom no early source used here names; Michael the Syrian and Bar Hebraeus say Thomas of Harkel later revised the New Testament after this first version, made at Mabbug through Philoxenus's care

keyWorks.title: Creed, anathemas and ten questions
keyWorks.about: short writings against Chalcedon and the two natures, which Budge quotes in his introduction; the first question asks to which of the two natures the Virgin gave birth

traces: Budge counts about ten British Museum manuscripts whose writers rank his authority on doctrine with that of Severus of Antioch, Cyril of Alexandria and Ephrem the Syrian.
Dionysius bar Salibi, a twelfth-century bishop of his church, names him among the "true and orthodox doctors and holy fathers", in Budge's English.

His sister's son, also named Philoxenus, went over to the Council of Chalcedon after his uncle died at Gangra and lived in Cyprus, Bar Hebraeus says, for a reason he will not write down; Michael the Syrian says the same and makes the nephew a bishop in Cyprus.
remembered: Severus of Antioch, in a letter to Julian of Halicarnassus that the Syriac chronicle under Zachariah's name copies, calls him "the memorable Akhs'noyo".
The Syriac Chronicle of 846 calls him a great teacher and a martyr. Bar Hebraeus calls him an eloquent man and a wonderful teacher.

His Chalcedonian opponents remembered him harshly. Theophanes the Confessor calls him Satan's slave and a follower of the Manichees, and Palestinian monks, in a letter Evagrius Scholasticus quotes, call him "truly a stranger to God".

Budge calls him "a merciless and relentless opponent" of those who differed from him on the natures of Christ, and says no final judgment on his character can be made until the case is stated from his own side.

uncertain: His years. No early source used here gives the year he was born or the year he died. Budge puts his birth in the third quarter of the fifth century. François Nau makes him bishop of Mabbug from 485 to 523, and the title page of Budge's translation gives 485 to 519. Budge dates a letter of 522 from his first exile at Philippopolis and puts the move to Gangra in the next year, but elsewhere calls the same letter one written in his second exile there. The Chronicle of 846 says he suffered martyrdom after many years of persecution.

The slave story. Theophanes the Confessor, writing for Chalcedon's side, says he was a Persian runaway slave who passed himself off as a cleric and was found unbaptized after he was made bishop. Budge says Theodore the Reader tells the same. Budge answers from Philoxenus's own words on his baptism, and calls the question of slavery a matter of no consequence.

How he died. The Syriac chronicle under Zachariah's name says he was imprisoned over the kitchen of the hostel at Gangra and suffocated by the smoke, as he says in his own letter, and that at last he died. The list of exiled bishops by John of Asia, as Michael the Syrian and Bar Hebraeus give it, says the smoke choked him there. An anonymous Life, which Budge quotes from Assemani, says the smoke was made on purpose in the room below a locked upper room. The Chronicle of 846 says he was shut in a furnace.

Calandion. Theophanes says Calandion of Antioch drove him out, and Budge follows this. The Syriac chronicle under Zachariah's name and Michael the Syrian say Philoxenus exposed Calandion and had him put out of his see.

Edessa. Budge says he studied there. The Chronicle of 846 says he had been one of the leaders of the school at Edessa, and that colleagues who envied him drove him out because he would not hold with Nestorius. Bar Hebraeus says the Persian teachers were driven from Edessa through his efforts.

The march on Antioch. Evagrius heard from very old men that monks stirred up by Xenaias rushed into Antioch and were killed in such numbers that many "found a grave in the Orontes". The chronicle under Zachariah's name, from his own side, says some were wounded and others killed.
Images. Theophanes says he taught that images of the Lord and the saints should be banned and removed, and Budge reports the charge. No source of his own church used here speaks of it.

His name. Theophanes says Peter the Fuller named him Philoxenus when he made him bishop, and Budge reports that the name was then changed from Akhsenaya. Evagrius says Xenaias was named Philoxenus in Greek.
